description: Hi, I’m Koushik, a software engineer in the Bay Area taking on the Earth System Trend Detective challenge solo. I’m building Earth Trend Detective: pick any place on Earth and it uses 45 years of NASA data to show what has really changed, tests whether each trend is real, and explains it in plain English. I care about clean design and AI you can actually trust. Always happy to connect with people who love climate data, stats or web development.
summary: Earth Trend Detective answers a simple question for any place on Earth: what has really changed here? Pick a location, and the app pulls 45 years of NASA POWER data (temperature, rainfall, humidity, soil moisture, sunlight and wind) and compares the last decade with 1981–2010. It tests every trend with Mann-Kendall and Sen’s slope, so people can tell real change from noise, and flags changes that moved together as possible drivers. You can also ask your own question, like “Are summers in Mountain View getting hotter?”. An AI detective plans the investigation, code runs every calculation, and every number in the answer is fact-checked against the NASA data before you see it. This matters because climate conversations are full of claims; this tool gives students, residents and planners honest, local evidence in plain English.
details:
Earth Trend Detective answers a question most people have but can’t easily check: what has actually changed where I live?

How it works: You pick any place on Earth. The app pulls 45 years of NASA POWER data for that spot, covering temperature, hottest days, coldest nights, rainfall, humidity, soil moisture, sunlight and wind. It compares the last 10 years with 1981–2010. Every trend gets a real statistical test (Mann-Kendall with Sen’s slope), so instead of “it feels hotter” you get “hottest days are rising 0.3 °C per decade, and that’s statistically significant.” It also shows which months changed most, and flags changes that moved together as possible drivers, like more sunlight alongside hotter days.

Ask the Detective: You can ask your own question in plain English, such as “Are summers in Mountain View getting hotter, and why?” The AI only does two jobs: it turns your question into a plan, and it writes the final answer. Everything in between is plain code: fetching the data, running the statistics, handling seasons (it knows summer in Sydney is December to February) and comparing places. Before you see the answer, a fact-checker matches every number the AI wrote against the real NASA data and removes any sentence it can’t verify. A “How it worked” tab shows each step, so nothing is a black box. When I asked about Mountain View, it honestly said no, average summers aren’t significantly hotter, but the hottest days and summer sunlight are rising.

What does this mean for me? You pick who you are (student, gardener, farmer, runner, parent, homeowner, outdoor worker or city planner) and get three practical takeaways plus one tip, all fact-checked.

Seen from space and climate stripes: For any place, the app shows real NASA satellite images from 2001 and 2025 side by side (vegetation greenness and daytime land temperature from MODIS on Terra, via NASA GIBS). It converts the image colors back into NASA’s actual values using GIBS’s published color tables, so it can say in plain words what changed, for example “Within 25 km of Mountain View, July 2025 was about as green as July 2001”, and map exactly where land got greener or browner. It also draws “climate stripes” for each place (one colored stripe per year since 1981) that people can download and share.

Benefits and impact: Climate conversations are full of claims and short on local evidence. This gives students something they can cite, residents an honest answer about home, and planners trends worth acting on. It says “no clear trend” when the data says so, which I think matters just as much as finding change.

Tools: TypeScript, Next.js, React, Tailwind CSS and Recharts, deployed on Vercel. Data comes from the NASA POWER API, place search from Open-Meteo, and the two language steps use Google Gemini. No hardware.

What makes it creative: Most AI climate tools let the model talk about numbers. I flipped that: code produces every number, the AI only writes the words, and a checker removes anything made up. The detective framing (case file, clues, verdict) makes statistics feel approachable instead of academic.

What I considered:

Accuracy: I recalculated Denver’s numbers independently from NASA’s raw API, and they matched to 4 decimal places. I also tested the Sahara, the South Pole, the Amazon, Mumbai’s monsoon, the open Pacific, a made-up town and a nonsense question.

Reliability: if NASA’s API is down, the app falls back to saved NASA data and labels it clearly.

Honesty about limits: NASA POWER is a roughly 50 km grid, so it shows regional climate, not your street. Trends show change, not proof of cause.
dataRefs: NASA POWER (Prediction Of Worldwide Energy Resources)
NASA POWER Monthly API (T2M, T2M_MAX, T2M_MIN, PRECTOTCORR, RH2M, GWETROOT, ALLSKY_SFC_SW_DWN, WS2M)
NASA GMAO MERRA-2 reanalysis (source of POWER meteorology)
NASA GIBS (Global Imagery Browse Services): MODIS Terra NDVI and land surface temperature imagery
projectRefs: Google Gemini API (question planning and plain-English answers)
